The primordial lithium abundance is still subject to significant uncertainty, with the measured value in metal-poor stars being three times lower than that predicted by standard Big Bang Nucleosynthesis.

The critical density for the transition to local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) is much higher for LiH (n_LiH,cr ~ 1.8 × 10^10 cm^-3) compared to H2 (n_H2,cr ~ 400 cm^-3) and HD (n_HD,cr ~ 6000 cm^-3) at T = 100 K.
The spontaneous-emission Einstein coefficient for the lowest-lying rotational transition of LiH, A_10(LiH) = 1.18 × 10^-2 s^-1, is much larger than that of HD, A_10(HD) = 5 × 10^-8 s^-1.
The maximum LiH abundance achieved in the simulations is only about [LiH/H] ~ 10^-9 at temperatures T < 100 K, even with the primordial lithium abundance enhanced by one order of magnitude.
The authors find that insufficient LiH is produced in all cases considered, with [LiH/Li] ~ 10^-9 at T < 100 K, due to the low abundance of neutral lithium Li^0.

The authors state that neglecting photo-destruction processes and potentially underestimating the collisional dissociation rate of LiH renders their results an extreme upper limit on the effect of LiH cooling.
For the case of shock-heated primordial gas with n_0 = 100 cm^-3, the gas cools to the CMB floor of T_CMB < 30 K in ~10^-2 t_H, where t_H is the Hubble time at z = 5, even without LiH cooling.
In the case of collapsing primordial gas in minihaloes and relic HII regions, the gas temperature does not reach the CMB floor, even with the maximal LiH cooling scenario.
The ratio of the cooling rates per molecule, W_LiH/W_HD, is around 10^-3 for n(H^0) ~ 10^6 cm^-3 at T = 40 K, below which the HD cooling efficiency rapidly drops.

The authors find that the cooling by LiH can safely be neglected for the thermal evolution of Population III star-forming gas, as its contribution is insignificant compared to other molecular coolants like H2 and HD.
